content: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a chronic condition affecting the pulmonary vasculature. It is one of several forms of pulmonary hypertension. The average age at which individuals are diagnosed with PAH is approximately 50 years. However, the prevalence of this condition increases significantly in individuals over the age of 70, with 10% to 17% of cases occurring in this age group. The median survival time for patients with PAH is estimated to be around seven years. Survival rates following diagnostic right-sided heart catheterization are reported to be 85% at one year, 68% at three years, 57% at five years, and 49% at seven years. Research has demonstrated that calcium channel blockers (CCBs) can reduce right ventricular hypertrophy and improve long-term hemodynamic parameters in patients with PAH. The objective of this review was to assess the clinical efficacy and potential harms associated with the use of CCBs in individuals diagnosed with PAH. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search strategy was employed, as provided by the Cochrane Airways Group Trials Search Coordinator. Databases searched included the Cochrane Airways Group Register of Trials, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Clinical Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, ClinicalTrials.gov, the WHO trial portal, and several Chinese biomedical databases such as CNKI, VIP Database, and WANFANG Database. The search covered studies from the inception of these databases up to September 2014. No restrictions were placed on language. The inclusion criteria for this review were fully published randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared CCBs with placebo or other treatments, or that evaluated CCBs as an adjunct to other therapies in patients with PAH. Standard Cochrane methods were used for data collection and analysis. Only one RCT was identified for inclusion in this review. However, this study was published solely in abstract form, and no data were available for evaluation. As a result, the efficacy and safety of CCBs in the treatment of PAH remain unproven due to the lack of robust evidence. Despite this, the search strategy identified four controlled clinical trials that were not randomized. Three of these studies suggested that treatment with CCBs might be beneficial for patients with PAH. Importantly, no adverse side effects associated with CCB use were reported in these studies. However, the findings from these non-randomized trials require confirmation through well-designed RCTs to establish the efficacy and safety of CCBs in this patient population.
